pronunciation.note: Adad is Tier 2: the Unicode restoration adds only capitalization and preserves no distinctive diacritic or non-Latin letter. The ASCII form 'adad' is historically identical to the standard Assyriological transliteration. PuniCodex keeps the capitalized form Adad as the canonical display name, but the temple is a reconstruction hub for the Mesopotamian storm god rather than a claim of domain ownership.

domains.title: ADAD — Lord of Thunder
domains.subtitle: Storm · Lightning · Rain · Divine Voice
domains.lead:
Adad is the Akkadian storm god, the lord of thunder and the divine voice that speaks in wind, rain, and lightning. In Sumerian he is Iškur; in the West Semitic world he is Addu or Hadad. Where Enlīl governs the wind and the cosmic decree, Adad is the storm's immediate, destructive, and life-giving power: the thunder that splits mountains, the flood that renews the plain, and the rain on which every Mesopotamian harvest depended.

This temple is a domainless flagship: the ASCII adad.com is unregistrable, so the restoration is displayed here without claiming ownership. The page functions as a philological and atmospheric reconstruction hub for one of the ancient Near East's most widely worshipped deities.

cards.name: Forked Lightning
cards.desc: The thunderbolt that splits the sky and reveals the god's presence in the storm cloud.

cards.name: The Thunder Bull
cards.desc: Bull and lion are Adad's animals; the bull's bellow is the thunder that rolls across the plain.

cards.name: Life-Giving Rain
cards.desc: Without Adad's winter rains the fields of Assyria and Babylonia would fail; the storm is also a fertility god.

cards.name: Thunder as Oracle
cards.desc: Adad and Šamaš preside over divination; thunder and lightning were read as the god's answer to human questions.

mythology.lead: Adad's myths are not narratives of courtship and descent like Ištar's; they are theophanies — descriptions of the storm's arrival, its terror, and its necessity. He appears in hymns, royal inscriptions, and the great flood epics as the voice that makes the earth tremble and the rain that decides whether a year will bring famine or plenty.

myths.title: The Hymn to Adad
myths.text: The Akkadian Hymn to Adad describes the god's arrival in the storm: the heavens thunder, the earth shakes, and his lightning flashes from one horizon to the other. He rides the storm winds; the mountains tremble before him. When Adad speaks in thunder, both gods and mortals listen. The hymn is not only praise but propaganda for kings who ruled by the god's mandate: to control Adad's cult was to claim access to the storm itself.

myths.title: Adad in the Deluge
myths.text: In the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, Utnapištim recounts the great flood: 'The gods of the abyss rose up; Nergal tore out the dam's bolt; Ninurta marched on and made the weirs overflow.' Adad's voice is the storm within the deluge; his thunder is the signal that the divine council has unleashed destruction upon the land. The storm god who brings rain in due season here becomes the agent of cosmic cleansing.

myths.title: Adad of Aleppo and Royal Treaty
myths.text: At Aleppo (Halab), the West Semitic storm god Addu was one of the most powerful deities of the Bronze Age Levant. The great kings of Mari, Yamkhad, and Hatti invoked him in treaties and royal correspondence; his thunder guaranteed oaths and his absence meant disaster. In the Middle Assyrian period Adad appears beside Aššur as a national god, granting the king victory in the field as surely as he granted rain to the field.

myths.title: Marduk Receives the Name Ramman
myths.text: In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Tablet VII, the gods bestow fifty names upon Marduk. One of them is Ramman, 'Thunderer' — an ancient epithet of Adad. By absorbing the storm god's name, Marduk assimilates the power of thunder and rain into his own kingship. The text is a theological charter: the local deity of Babylon becomes lord of the storm because the older storm god's essence has been transferred to him.

syncretism: The Sumerian storm god Iškur and the Akkadian Adad were identified with one another from an early date; in bilingual texts and god lists they function as a single deity with two names. In the West Semitic world he was Addu or Hadad, a major god of Aleppo and the Syrian steppe, and his imagery influenced the Canaanite storm-god Baal. The Hurrian and Hittite storm god Teššub was equated with Adad in diplomatic and religious correspondence. In later periods Adad's thundering role was absorbed into Marduk (as Ramman in the Enuma Elish) and, through cultural diffusion, into the broader ancient Near Eastern image of the storm-god who rides the clouds and wields the lightning.
culturalLegacy: Adad's legacy is the idea that weather is a form of speech. In Mesopotamian thought thunder was not mere noise but the god's voice; rain was not mere hydrology but a divine gift. This theology shaped royal ideology across the Near East: the king who maintained Adad's cult could claim that the skies themselves endorsed his rule. The name survives in biblical and later Semitic studies as Hadad/Adad, and the imagery of the storm-god — bull, lightning, and rain — passed into Canaanite, Israelite, and eventually classical iconography. PuniCodex restores Adad as a Tier-2 reconstruction: there are no hidden diacritics, only the name itself, still rolling like thunder across four thousand years.
extendedMeditation:
Every storm is a theophany for those who know how to read it. Adad is the deity of that reading: the god whose presence is announced by darkening sky, by the first cold drop, by the flash that divides the horizon and the silence that follows before the thunder. He is not a god of hidden places but of open air; his temple is the whole sky above the Mesopotamian plain.

The name Adad is onomatopoeic in its way — two sharp syllables, the second echoing the first, like thunder answering lightning. The Sumerians called him Iškur, the Akkadians Adad, the people of Aleppo Addu, and the Hittites saw him in Teššub. Each name is a local dialect of the same overwhelming experience: the sky has a voice, and it is not indifferent. To restore Adad in Unicode is not to add a diacritic but to keep the capital letter upright against the wind, a small flag claiming that even a name without fancy marks deserves its temple.

archaeology: Storm-god imagery is widespread across Mesopotamia and the Levant. At Aleppo, the temple of the storm god Addu was a major Bronze Age sanctuary; cylinder seals and stelae show the god brandishing a forked lightning or standing on a bull. In Assyria, Adad appears in royal inscriptions and palace reliefs as a patron of the king's wars. Cuneiform copies of the Enuma Elish and Akkadian hymns from Nineveh, Assur, and Babylon preserve the theological tradition by which Adad's thunder was transferred to Marduk as the name Ramman.
